```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5
)
library(reach.rate)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
```

**Audience:** novice. You have a file of spot gaugings and want a rating
from it. No knowledge of the package, of S7 or of the mathematics is assumed;
terms are explained where they first appear, and `vignette("glossary")` lists
them all.

This page takes one file from start to finish. The file is synthetic, a made-up
station called Example Weir, in the layout of an Environment Agency gauging
export. It has a few faults in it on purpose, because a real archive does, and
you will see what the package does about each.

<pre class="mermaid">
flowchart LR
  A[Your file] --> B[read_gaugings<br/>read it, keep every row]
  B --> C[validate_gaugings<br/>is it usable, does it look right]
  C --> D[fit_rating<br/>fit, and record how]
  D --> E[assess_rating<br/>look from six sides]
  D --> F[autoplot<br/>draw it]
  E --> G[apply_rating<br/>stage to discharge]
  F --> G
  G --> H[A person reviews<br/>and decides]
</pre>

The diagram shows the route. Every step keeps what the one before found, and
none of them removes a row from your data. At the end a person decides whether
the rating is fit to use. The package never makes that decision for you.

# Your file

```{r file}
path <- system.file("extdata", "example_gaugings.csv", package = "reach.rate")
cat(readLines(path, n = 6), sep = "\n")
```

Each row is one spot gauging: a stage in metres and a discharge in cubic metres
per second, measured together at one time. A **rating curve** is the
relationship between them, so that a stage reading, which is easy to measure
continuously, can be turned into a discharge, which is not.

# Read it

```{r read}
gaugings <- read_gaugings(path)
```

`read_gaugings()` reads every column as text and then turns it into numbers and
dates one step at a time, so that a problem is noted on its own row and not
silently dropped or changed. It tells you what it found:

```{r read-summary}
read_summary(gaugings)
gaugings[!is.na(read_issue), .(source_row, stage_original, discharge_original, read_issue)]
```

`---` is a placeholder for "no value" and `1.60m` has a unit stuck to it. Both
are kept, with the original text beside them, and each row says what was wrong.
Nothing has been removed or corrected.

# Check it

```{r validate}
checks <- validate_gaugings(gaugings, reference_time = as.POSIXct("2025-01-01", tz = "UTC"))
checks
```

There are two kinds of finding. A **fail** means the data cannot be used as it
stands, such as a stage that is not a number. A **warning** is a judgement for
you to make, such as a gauging that is far from its neighbours. The check never
removes anything; it names the rows concerned so you can look.

```{r validate-detail}
assessment_checks(checks)[status %in% c("fail", "warning"), .(check_id, status, message)]
plot(checks)
```

Look at the two rows the outlier and zero-discharge checks point to before you
go on. In a real archive you would go back to the paper record. Here we know
one was entered 60% too high and one is a dry pool.

# Fit a rating

```{r fit}
fit <- fit_rating(gaugings)
fit
```

`fit_rating()` makes choices a careful analyst would not argue with, and says
what they were. It fits **one limb**, one equation
$Q = C\,(H - a)^n$ over the whole range, because a rating with several limbs is
a decision about the river that you should make, not the software. It fits on
the **relative** objective, because gauging error is usually proportional to the
reading. And it leaves out the rows it cannot use, listing each with its reason:

```{r excluded}
rating_provenance(fit)$fit_rating$excluded[, .(evidence_id, reason)]
```

The printed rating also says whether the optimiser **converged** and whether the
equations are **valid**. They are separate questions, and both should be yes.

# Look at it

```{r plot}
autoplot(fit)
```

The curve runs through the gaugings. Evidence that is not a gauging would have
a different shape, and rows left out of the fit are drawn grey and faint, not
hidden. The caption gives the rating's status.

# Assess it

```{r assess}
assessment <- assess_rating(fit, reference_time = as.POSIXct("2025-01-01", tz = "UTC"))
assessment
```

`assess_rating()` looks at the rating from six sides: the **data**, the
**numerical** behaviour of the fit, the **statistical** quality, the
**hydraulic** plausibility, the **operational** limits and the **provenance**.
There is no score. A single number would hide exactly the things a reviewer needs
to see, so each check says what it found and what to look at next. Read the
ones that did not pass:

```{r assess-detail}
assessment_checks(assessment)[status %in% c("warning", "fail"), .(domain, check_id, message)]
```

# Use it

```{r apply}
apply_rating(fit, c(0.5, 1.2, 2.5))
```

The `support` column says what each answer rests on. `interpolation_observed`
means the stage lies among the gaugings, which is the best case.

Forecast models need discharge above the highest gauging, so a rating made by
`fit_rating()` does not stop at the edge of its evidence. Ask for a stage
beyond it and you get an answer, flagged, with a warning:

```{r extrapolate}
out <- withCallingHandlers(
  apply_rating(fit, c(2.5, 3.6)),
  warning = function(w) {
    message("Warning: ", conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
out
```

The 3.6 m row is marked `extrapolation`. The value rests on the equation alone,
with no gauging beyond 2.9 m to check it. Use it, and say so.

You can turn that flag into a boundary. If you know where the rating may be
used, such as a structure's limit or a surveyed control, say so and say why:

```{r limits-set, error=TRUE}
limited <- set_operational_limits(fit, 0.25, 3.6, basis = "control confirmed by survey to 3.6 m")
apply_rating(limited, c(2.5, 3.6))
apply_rating(limited, 4.2)
```

Inside the limits you still get flagged extrapolation. Outside them the rating
refuses, because that range was your decision and the package holds you to it.

# How sure is it?

The quick question is how much one gauging matters. `rating_sensitivity()`
leaves gaugings out and refits, and reports the effect on discharge:

```{r sensitivity}
sens <- rating_sensitivity(fit, tests = "leave_high_out", stages = c(1, 2, 3))
sens
```

Leaving out the highest gaugings moves the top of the curve most, which is what
you would expect, since the top is the part with the fewest gaugings behind it.

# What is not here yet

`export_rating()`, to write a rating and its assessment out for others to review,
is planned and not built. Until it is, the rating object itself, saved with
`saveRDS()`, carries everything: the evidence with its ids, how it was fitted,
what was left out and why, and its status.

The lifecycle of every rating starts at `draft` and the package never moves it
on. Approval is a decision for a person.
